title: Sleep: insomnia in its own right or as part of something else
about: Questions that tell apart insomnia as a problem in its own right from poor sleep driven by mood, worry, nightmares, substances, a medical problem or the schedule, and that check for sleep apnea, restless legs, a late body clock, dream enactment and a reduced need for sleep (mood elevation).

questions.text: Is poor sleep a problem in its own right, or mostly the result of something else, such as low mood, worry, nightmares, pain, a medical problem, alcohol, caffeine or shift work?
questions.why: Insomnia that persists in its own right responds well to CBT for insomnia, even alongside other problems. Sleep driven by nightmares, substances, a medical problem or the work schedule calls for those to be addressed directly.

options.label: A problem in its own right
Mostly low mood or worry
options.note: Treat the mood or worry pattern; CBT for insomnia can still help if poor sleep persists.

options.label: Mostly alcohol, caffeine or other substances
Mostly pain, breathing problems or another medical issue
Shift work or an irregular schedule
options.note: Consider a circadian rhythm problem; schedule-focused sleep advice comes first.

questions.text: How many nights a week is sleep poor, and for how long has this been going on?
questions.why: Poor sleep on most nights for months is a different problem from a rough patch of a few weeks, which often settles once the trigger passes. It also sets the duration used for the other patterns.

options.label: Most nights, for 6 months or more
Most nights, for under a month
Only now and then
options.note: Occasional poor sleep is common; sleep habits advice may be enough.

questions.text: Does the client snore loudly, stop breathing or gasp in sleep (as a bed partner may notice), or feel very sleepy in the daytime despite enough time in bed?
questions.why: Sleep apnea often sits behind tiredness, poor sleep and low mood, and it changes the plan: it needs a medical or sleep medicine assessment.

options.label: Yes
options.note: Suggest a primary care or sleep medicine assessment for possible sleep apnea.

questions.text: On nights with little sleep, is the client tired the next day, or unusually full of energy despite sleeping little?
questions.why: Feeling charged rather than tired after little sleep can signal mood elevation, which changes the picture and the plan; tiredness after poor sleep fits insomnia.

options.label: Unusually full of energy
options.note: Ask about other signs of mood elevation and consider a psychiatric evaluation.

questions.text: Does anything else disturb the night: an urge to move the legs in the evening that eases with movement, a body clock that runs very late (sleeps well if allowed to sleep in), frequent nightmares, or acting out dreams?
questions.why: Restless legs, a delayed body clock, nightmare disorder and dream enactment each need their own assessment, often with sleep medicine, and they change whether sleep restriction is suitable.

options.label: An urge to move the legs at rest that eases with movement
options.note: Possible restless legs: suggest a primary care or sleep medicine review.

options.label: Falls asleep very late but sleeps well when allowed to sleep in
options.note: Possible delayed sleep-wake phase: schedule and timed-light advice, often with sleep medicine, comes before sleep restriction.

options.label: Frequent nightmares that wake them up
options.note: Nightmares respond to imagery rehearsal or trauma-focused care (AASM position paper, 2018).

options.label: Acts out dreams, sleepwalks or gets hurt at night
